title: K3 Has No Disruptive Innovation, but Pushes Activated Parameters to the 100B Scale
dek: Sun Yutao reads the Kimi K3 technical report, pointing out that it has no single breakthrough but rather fuses existing techniques such as linear attention, hybrid attention, and dynamic load balancing to achieve activated parameters at the 100B scale; he judges that large models will see no more Transformer-level innovations, only incremental improvements.
why: Extremely information-dense, the guest connects over a dozen papers to explain the ins and outs of the K3 architecture, offering direct judgments on hot topics like MLA, WSD, and positional encoding.
who: Large-model architecture researchers, pretraining and inference engineers, and anyone wanting to understand Kimi K3's technical decisions and the latest industry trends in architecture fusion.

points.h: Architecture improvements no longer chase performance, only inference efficiency
points.body: Sun Yutao points out that in the era of large models, parameter count is the primary factor for performance, and the performance gains from architectural improvements are relatively small; however, different architectures show huge differences in inference efficiency, which directly determines deployment cost. Industry research has therefore shifted from performance-oriented to efficiency-oriented, focusing on inference efficiency. His doctoral research, starting in 2023, mainly addresses inefficiencies in large-model inference, including linear attention and hybrid attention.

points.h: Hybrid attention is an engineering compromise, yet capability is not lost
points.body: Although hybrid attention is an engineering compromise architecturally, it is not a compromise in model performance. As long as a certain proportion of full attention is maintained, the model can achieve lossless or even better upper bounds—meaning engineering gains without sacrificing the capability of full attention. This experimental conclusion has led to the widespread adoption of hybrid attention. However, Sun also notes its limitation: the inference speedup is proportional to the hybrid ratio. For example, when full attention occupies one quarter, the speedup is also limited by that, representing a constant-factor improvement, which is why he later turned to shared-KV architectures.

points.h: Parameter count remains the most essential variable determining intelligence ceiling
points.body: Kimi K3's core selling point is effective scaling: total parameters of 2.8T, activated parameters around 100B, and context length reaching the 1M scale. Sun emphasizes that larger models have higher intelligence ceilings, and parameter size remains the most essential variable for model intelligence. At release, K3 was much larger than other domestic open-source models and was one of the earliest models to successfully reach this scale.

points.h: MLA is nothing new, just an equivalent implementation of MQA
points.body: Regarding V4's abandonment of MLA, Sun believes MLA is essentially an equivalent form of MQA, bringing nothing new but a better implementation path. MLA's benefits mainly come from parameter design; its computation is far greater than actually needed, wasting compute during inference. Lu Fuli felt that on inference chips, MTP could utilize compute more effectively, so V4 switched to MTP. He thinks this is not a matter of right or wrong but a choice. K3 retains MLA because K2's priority was getting things to work; if it works, don't change it. It may not continue to be used in the future.

points.h: When splitting two matrices, normalization must be inserted between them
points.body: Sun proposes an architectural design principle: two matrices multiplied together can be merged into one in terms of expressiveness, but they are not equivalent in optimization properties, often leading to training instability. Therefore, if two matrices must be written separately, a normalization must be added between them to stabilize training. This occurs in MLA and the two-layer matrices in FFN. He also mentions that using clip to directly truncate intermediate activations is a crude approach; a smoother approach is to constrain intermediate activations to a mathematically controllable range via normalization.

points.h: Today's Transformer is already a Ship of Theseus
points.body: Sun believes that current model training does not involve a huge, so-called disruptive innovation but rather fuses many previous works to find better combinations. He uses the Ship of Theseus as a metaphor for the Transformer: the 2017 ship was assembled from parts like attention and MLP, and over eight or nine years of sailing, some parts have been continuously replaced, so today's similarity to the original is very low. Whether it is still called a Transformer is a philosophical question, but from an engineering perspective, people still call it that. Technology improves gradually, driven by everyone.

points.h: WSD does not reduce tuning difficulty; K3 chose a simpler scheme
points.body: Sun introduces the WSD learning rate schedule proposed by MiniMax: during the cooldown phase, the model learns fastest, so high-quality data can be concentrated there, achieving better results than uniformly distributing data. WSD also allows freely switching the actual token count during training, making it easier to adjust release timing. However, the K3 team believes WSD's tuning difficulty is not reduced because the optimal cooldown ratio still depends on the total token count; they chose a simpler scheme with only two variables (total token count and peak learning rate), which is easier to tune.

points.h: Large models may never see another Transformer-level innovation
points.body: Sun offers a bold claim: large models may not see innovations like the Transformer itself; everything after will be incremental improvements. He believes that as long as a capability can be clearly defined, it can be achieved; pure language models reaching AGI is not a big problem, but AGI involving interaction with the real physical world still has a long way to go. Model size cannot grow indefinitely because the amount of information that can be aggregated on the human internet is finite, so models need not be infinitely large. He also mentions that because the room for improvement in large models is limited, he personally has turned to exploring world models.

quotes.text: I think K3 is quite bold—on the basis of existing open-source models, they aim to raise it by an order of magnitude.
My view is that scientific research does not have leapfrogging improvements. It's just that people tend to mark certain nodes of incremental improvement as milestones.
Let me give my judgment—my judgment is a bold claim. My paradox is that large models may not have innovations like the Transformer itself; everything after will be incremental improvements.
